title: Pro$^2$ Agent: Scientific Problem Probing for Autonomous AI R&D
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now autonomously conduct AI research by writing code and running experiments. They typically do so by iteratively optimizing a codebase, while ignoring the problem structure behind the task. This formulation is effective on simpler tasks, but on difficult problems it often gets stuck in the wrong solution region because the agent never explicitly represents its understanding of the problem. We introduce Pro$^2$ Agent, which shifts the primary state of autonomous AI research from a codebase state to a Problem State: an explicit structure of what problems prevent success and which solutions are likely to address them. Pro$^2$ Agent initializes the Problem State through comprehensive analysis of available resources and constraints. It then performs targeted research to relate the identified problems to candidate solutions. Through controlled hypothesis testing, the agent updates the importance of a suspected problem or the benefit brought by a candidate solution. On the complete MLE-Bench, Pro$^2$ Agent matches the best reported medal rate (70.7%) under the standard 24-hour budget and reaches 76.0% with a 48-hour budget, the highest medal rate reported on the complete benchmark. It also achieves competitive performance on PostTrainBench. In addition, it produces research notes for each task that make the research process transparent and reusable by human researchers.

title: JARVIS: An Agent That Designs, Builds, and Tests Circuit Boards on Its Own
abstract: Power electronics is central to the energy transition, but developing new hardware still relies on human-led design, fabrication, testing, and iteration. We present JARVIS, an embodied AI agent that autonomously closes this loop for circuit boards. JARVIS maintains machine-specific capabilities and constraints, scans its workspace using a robot-mounted 3D scanner, and constructs an executable digital twin in which it rehearses robot motions, fabrication steps, and circuit behavior before consuming materials. A single text instruction initiates the physical experiment. Using unmodified desktop equipment, the agent coordinates a robot arm, a PCB printer that deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste, and a pick-and-place machine. It verifies progress using cameras and sensors, then tests the fabricated circuit with an OPAL-RT real-time simulator and an oscilloscope. Based on the measurements, JARVIS diagnoses deviations from the design and generates a revised design in KiCad for subsequent rehearsal. In a demonstration involving a 60 Hz notch filter for grid-connected converter sensing, JARVIS completed a first-run experiment in 2 h 39 min without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. Its digital-twin rehearsal identified five issues before fabrication, including a test criterion that would have incorrectly rejected a functioning board. During execution, the agent also resolved encountered faults autonomously. These results demonstrate an integrated agent-driven workflow for physical design, fabrication, measurement, and iterative improvement of power-electronic circuitry. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power electronics in which an agent closes the physical design-build-test-learn loop for circuit boards.

title: On the Reliability of CyberGym Evaluation: Task Material Consistency and Reference-Target Identity
abstract: CyberGym evaluates vulnerability reproduction by checking whether a proof-of-concept input (PoC) crashes a vulnerable program version but not a fixed version. Interpreting this differential pass as successful reproduction requires consistent task materials and evidence that the PoC triggers the intended defect. We examine these requirements through a material audit of all 1,507 CyberGym tasks and an identity assessment of the final PoCs from one complete Level-1 GLM-5.3 run. Taking the defect associated with each reference crash report as the target, the audit assigns inconsistency labels to 338 tasks (22.4%) after correcting two labels identified by stratified blind review. The largest categories are coverage inconsistency (205 tasks) and descriptions and patches that jointly point to another defect (110 tasks). We assess PoC identity using an execution check, crash-signature matching, and LLM-assisted root-cause review. Of the 1,286 differential passes, the procedure assigns 89 non-target and 10 insufficient-evidence verdicts; requiring a target hit lowers the pass rate from 85.3% to 78.8%. Non-target verdicts also occur in tasks with no material inconsistency found: 39 of 1,052 differential passes (3.7%). Although the identity verdicts require independent validation, these findings motivate separate checks of task-material consistency and submission identity when interpreting vulnerability-reproduction scores.

title: Aggron: Aggressive Compression of Agentic KV Caches during Head-of-Line Stalls in the Request Queue
abstract: LLM agents run long, multi-turn programs whose contexts grow at every step, and serving them is limited by KV cache capacity. To alleviate this limitation, systems use context compression techniques, which typically wait until the KV cache crosses a large threshold and then summarize large spans of history at once, either in the background while the agent progresses or on the critical path. These summarizations can be done using the same model running on the same engine, or using the same or a different model running on extra hardware. When running on the same engine, summarization competes with the requests being served for both compute and memory capacity. To maximize the cost-effectiveness of summarization, this paper presents a new serving system called {\em Aggron}. Aggron summarizes agentic requests at every turn and selectively summarizes only certain parts of the KV cache. As a result, Aggron retains accuracy and keeps summarization requests lightweight. Moreover, Aggron launches summarization requests from a separate {\em Summarization Queue} while the corresponding agentic request whose KV cache we want to compress is stalled in the main request queue due to head-of-line stalls. The Summarization queue utilizes compute and memory capacity left over by the head-of-line stalls in the main queue. Further, to maximize efficiency, the server issues summarizations only when it predicts that they can complete before the corresponding agentic request will finally execute. In our evaluation, we compare Aggron to state-of-the-art asynchronous summarization. At high load, Aggron reduces P99 program latency by $27$--$31\%$, and raises throughput by $1.34$--$1.40\times$.

title: TriageGPT for DataOps: Large Language Models as Intelligent Incident Classification and Resolution Agents in Data Pipeline Operations
abstract:
Purpose: This paper presents TriageGPT for DataOps, an architecture in which large language model agents classify data pipeline incidents, retrieve relevant context, and perform constrained autonomous remediation, in order to reduce the manual triage effort that drives incident duration and on-call fatigue. 
Methodology: TriageGPT combines a retrieval-augmented classification agent that assigns alerts to a data pipeline specific incident taxonomy, a tool-use resolution agent that invokes actions from a vetted, blast-radius-tiered action library, and an audit-logged guardrail layer that gates and can automatically roll back actions, paired with confidence-based human-in-the-loop escalation. We describe the architecture, algorithms and calibration policy, map the design to safety and governance guidance, and report a prototype evaluation on a benchmark pipeline with a fourteen-category taxonomy, 2,800 labeled synthetic incidents and a twelve-week comparative deployment trial. 
Findings: TriageGPT achieved 94.3 percent top-one classification accuracy and 95.1 percent factual attribution accuracy with retrieval, against 68.4 percent without it. It resolved 71.5 percent of test incidents without human intervention at an incorrect-action rate of 0.6 percent, every one of which the guardrail caught and reversed. In the deployment trial it reduced median time to resolution from 41 minutes under manual on-call practice to 9.8 minutes. 
Unique Contribution to Theory, Policy and Practice: For theory, the paper treats autonomous remediation as something earned through calibrated confidence and bounded blast radius rather than assumed. For practice, it provides an architecture, algorithms and evaluation method for resolving routine pipeline incidents while deferring the rest to a human with an evidence-grounded case. For policy, it maps autonomous remediation to existing guidance, informing how organizations set guardrails, audit requirements and risk tolerance for AIOps agents.

title: Reducing Inference Cost of Coding Agents with Timeout Cascades
abstract: AI coding agents have become one of the most popular applications of large language models. Yet, agentic AI comes at the cost of a tremendous amount of GPU compute resources, which limits its profitability and its viability at scale. In this paper, we investigate whether smaller, cheaper models can cut this cost without sacrificing accuracy. We evaluate 36 popular large and small open-weight models released since 2024 on a software engineering benchmark, and find that recent small models are closing the accuracy gap compared to their large counterparts. We investigate the structure of this gap and find that the gap is highly concentrated around hard tasks that small language models fail to solve while achieving remarkably good accuracy for easy and medium complexity tasks. Following this observation, we show that by utilizing a hybrid inference strategy that tries a small model first and escalates to a large one only when needed, we can achieve up to 33% reduction in total GPU-hour costs and 16.4% on all tasks from SWE-bench Verified, without sacrificing accuracy. Strikingly, this simple cascade nearly matches an oracle-style task router, highlighting a practical path for deploying cost-aware coding agents in production without complex learned task routers and with minimal engineering complexity.

title: Semantic Context Handoff with On-Demand Evidence for Long-Horizon Agents
abstract: Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. As execution proceeds, this history keeps growing, increasing inference cost and potentially degrading accuracy. Existing methods control this growth by preserving compact conclusions while removing earlier observations, but doing so can discard evidence that later becomes relevant. We introduce Semantic Context Handoff (SCH), whose central abstraction is state--evidence separation: a compact semantic state carries the agent's current interpretation, while supporting action--observation evidence remains separately addressable and can re-enter context when later execution makes it relevant, without separate summarization or retrieval-model calls. Empirically, SCH improves long-horizon agent performance while substantially reducing context cost. In a controlled 150-task SWE-bench study, SCH's evidence recovery improves Pass@1 from $80.0\%$ to $86.9\%$ at essentially unchanged token use and execution time. In the complete-system comparison, SCH achieves 86.9% Pass@1 while using 43% fewer tokens and 41% less wall-clock time than the strongest baseline by task performance. Across models and benchmarks, SCH consistently reduces token use relative to full-history prompting while remaining competitive with or improving upon the evaluated baselines. Trajectory analysis confirms that SCH recovers evidence from substantially earlier parts of the interaction history rather than merely preserving a recent context window.

title: Keeping Up with the Kernel: Can LLMs Adapt Linux Drivers to Interface Changes?
abstract: We analyze collateral evolution in Linux, the coordinated updates that drivers require when the kernel interfaces they depend on change, over the 20 years since it was first studied, covering releases from v3.0 to v7.2. Since v2.6.13, the number of driver files and support libraries has grown about eightfold, a single change to the most widely used library can now reach about 5.3k driver files, and such changes arrive either in bursts or spread over many releases. We introduce CoEvoBench, a benchmark that asks models to adapt an old driver module to a target kernel and evaluates the result against the developer's reference patch. The benchmark contains 316 manually confirmed tasks from 202 mainline commits and 268 modules, spanning kernel releases v6.19 to v7.2. It distinguishes 134 build-breaking tasks, where the old driver fails to compile, from 182 build-compatible tasks, where the old usage still builds. Using CoEvoAgent, we evaluate Direct, SmPL, and mini-SWE-agent with DeepSeek Flash, and compare Direct with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol. With DeepSeek, default Direct generation achieves strict reference agreement on 41.0% of build-breaking tasks but only 3.3% of build-compatible tasks.

title: 3D GameDev Arena: Benchmarking Coding Agents That Plan, Build, and Playtest extreme Long-Horizon Browser Games
abstract: Coding agents now resolve repository issues and generate compact playable games, but whether they can build a large 3D game from scratch remains open. Such games tightly couple mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic, and their quality rests on player enjoyment, which existing benchmarks rarely assess. Thus, we introduce 3D GameDev Arena, a first extreme long-horizon benchmark of 108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres. Given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images, a fully automated plan--implement--test--repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game. Runs average $\sim$1,000 LLM calls ; the longest uses 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets. Evaluation spans (1) objective code-level functional acceptance against the game specification, (2) agent-based QA and playtesting of 3D presentation and playability, and (3) blind pairwise Bradley-Terry human preference in a public arena. The preliminary findings indicate that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved, and code-level correctness alone does not dictate player preference. The public arena is hosted online.

title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance
abstract: Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent

title: Attestation is All You Need: Toward a Zero-Trust Architecture for HPC AI Agents
abstract: AI agents are beginning to automate data analysis, orchestration, and simulation steering in HPC environments, but they introduce a security problem that existing cluster defenses do not address: the hijacked authorized agent. An adversary can subvert an agent through prompt injection, poisoned shared data, compromised tools, or multi-agent coordination, then exfiltrate sensitive data through legitimate encrypted LLM API traffic. We propose behavioral attestation as a runtime defense for this setting. Our system, AEGIS, compiles task-derived behavioral constraints, monitors agent actions with ebpf-based syscall interception, verifies evidence against constraint profiles, correlates behavior across agents, and triggers slurm-level containment. On the real attestation path, AEGIS detects all four implemented attack classes with sub-second median latency at a 1-second interval and low measured verifier overhead. Controlled experiments show full attack-suite coverage, stronger detection than representative baselines, and no observed false positives on the evaluated benign workflows.

title: ShellBench: What Matters More for AI Agents, Models, or Harness for Everyday Tasks
abstract: The use of AI agents among the general public has been increasing exponentially throughout 2026, though it is often hard for users to determine which configuration is most effective for their personal use. To help provide clarity here we introduce ShellBench, 100 day-to-day tasks based on more than 10 million user requests, each set in a realistic workspace with messy files and competing data sources, and graded for both correctness and safety. We evaluate 12 models across 5 agent harnesses at 3 reasoning levels for a total of 53,100 rollouts, 20% of which are on tasks designated for public release. We find that model choice impacts performance more than harness choice, but the three leading models differ by only 1.1 percentage points. GPT-6.1 Sol passed 61.4% of attempts at about one-sixth of GPT-6 Astra's estimated token cost per attempt, while GPT-6 Astra led at 62.5%. We also found that harness choice had little effect on either performance or safety with all harnesses scoring between 42.9 (Claude Code) and 45.2 (OpenClaw) for pass@1.

title: Interactive Neural Computers
abstract: Computers and their interfaces are usually treated as fixed, so a person, or increasingly an AI agent, must adapt to whatever the operating system presents. This is limiting when someone needs a different workflow, or an interface suited to hands-free use or a disability. We explore an overlooked alternative. Rather than training an agent to operate an existing computer, we train a generative model to be the computer, predicting each next screen from past screens and the user's mouse and keyboard actions. Treating a desktop as an interactive world model raises problems that natural-video world models largely avoid. Without a camera pose to index memory, the model must remember content that has left the screen without any geometric cues. Arithmetic in a terminal has to be exactly right, not merely plausible. Small interface text must also stay legible at interactive frame rates. Our Interactive Neural Computer is structured like a Neural Turing Machine and starts to address these problems with three modules trained end to end from pixels and actions. A surprise-gated slot memory, supervised by latent next-frame prediction (MEMORY-JEPA), stores what is off screen. An exploratory query bridge brings in the reasoning of a pretrained VLM, and a residual renderer predicts only the latent changes between frames. In long closed-loop rollouts, our model recalls occluded files in 64.2% of trials (chance is 33.3%), compared with at most 56.0% for recurrent and sliding-window baselines. It also raises terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%. Finally, because the memory is explicit, it can be transplanted at test time to causally change what the model renders.

title: CAPTA: Identifying LLMs Behind AI Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents access remote services through tools to complete user tasks, often via API calls. In this setting, a remote service may want to identify the backend LLM of an agent to launch model-specific attacks, including prompt injection or selective delivery of manipulated content. However, the service cannot directly query the backend model and must instead collect observable responses through its interactions with the agent, making identification challenging.   In this paper, we present Completely Automated Preference Test to tell LLMs Apart (CAPTA), a model identification approach inspired by CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart), which distinguishes humans from automated programs. CAPTA presents multiple-choice questions as verification challenges, using differences in models' selection preferences to identify the backend LLM. It selects questions based on cross-model option-generation diversity and uses LLM-guided search to optimize their option sets. Our evaluation shows that CAPTA achieves 99.0% mean identification accuracy with only 10 questions across 25 LLMs from 10 model families. We further evaluate CAPTA with four widely used agents and seven representative LLMs, achieving 99.7% mean identification accuracy across all 28 agent-LLM combinations with 30 submitted answers.

title: Bathys: Advancing Deep Search Agents
abstract: Deep search is a critical capability for agents tackling complex, open-ended tasks, where solving a problem requires iterative information gathering, query reformulation, and evidence-based verification rather than a single retrieval step. To address these requirements, we present Bathys 9B and 27B deep search agents built around a training framework that spans verifiable question synthesis, post-training, and online reinforcement learning (RL) under context compression. Our high-quality data construction ensures both search depth and reliability: each clue is reformulated as an indirect reference requiring independent retrieval, and retained evidence chains enable verification that the clues jointly determine a unique answer. Curated trajectories underpin a pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO), and Compaction-Managed Group Sequence Policy Optimization (CM-GSPO): SFT provides a stable foundation for tool use over long horizons and query reformulation; KTO uses binary feedback on trajectories to improve the selection of answers grounded in evidence; CM-GSPO optimizes execution sub-trajectories with length-normalized likelihood ratios on the recorded rollout contexts and reweights sub-trajectory advantages to correct the extra weighting introduced by independently averaging sub-trajectory losses. Bathys 9B and 27B attain 66.51% and 80.49% on BrowseComp, respectively, under an evaluation protocol with trajectory self-verification and conditional retries.

title: ICLWorld: Benchmarking In-Context Learning of Agents from Digital to Physical Worlds
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets agents acquire new rules from context and adapt to user-specific requirements at inference time. The same frontier agents now operate both computers and robots, yet their ICL remains insufficiently assessed: existing benchmarks are largely offline, rely on text or static images, and risk training-data contamination, while robot evaluations are limited to method-level ablations. We present ICLWorld, an online benchmark that evaluates the ICL of agents from digital to physical worlds, covering computer use and robot use, together with UIverse, a unified harness that turns every environment into a user interface. We build 30 environments, record 630 demonstration videos (10+ hours), and design 160 tasks with customized, often counter-intuitive rules that cannot be satisfied without learning from the context. Each task comes with three rule versions, given as text or video, and we test generalization at three levels, from replaying the demonstration to new instances and unseen environments. Across six frontier models, the strongest agents, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, succeed on 82% and 76% of computer-use runs but only 27% and 26% of robot-use runs, and a no-rule control reduces success to at most 8%. GPT-6 Astra succeeds under all three rule versions on only 38% of computer-use tasks, half its rate under a single rule, and answers 98% of robot rule questions correctly yet completes only 20% of these tasks. Frontier agents learn rules comparably well from video and from text and transfer them across environments, whereas weaker agents rely on text and lose most of their video-based success once the demonstrated situation is resampled. These findings reveal substantial gaps between the digital and the physical world and between identifying a rule and acting on it.

title: Next-Manip: On-Demand Agent-Policy Collaboration for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: General-purpose robotic manipulation requires task reasoning, failure recovery, and precise control, yet limited manipulation data make these abilities difficult to obtain from a single policy. Recent multimodal agents show promise in task reasoning and recovery but lack reliable fine-grained control and incur high inference cost, whereas learned policies provide efficient fine-grained execution but struggle beyond their learned skills. Although their complementary strengths suggest combining the two, doing so requires repeatedly deciding which executor should act as task demands change. Instead of relying on the agent for each decision, we present Next-Manip, an on-demand agent--policy collaboration framework that decouples executor allocation from costly agent inference. We propose an Agent Invocation Controller (AIC) that allocates control between the policy and the agent through a lightweight classifier of current execution demands. We further introduce Task Dynamics Context (TDC), which packages informative manipulation changes from in-context examples into compact task references to support both agent reasoning and executor allocation. Across two simulation benchmarks and real-world experiments, Next-Manip achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing agent inference costs.

title: VISE: Verifier-Independent Skill Self-Evolution with Feedback from Tool Implementations
abstract: Agent skills provide reusable workflows that guide LLM agents in using tools. Refining these workflows requires feedback on missing or incorrect instructions, but task-specific verifiers are not always available. We propose VISE (Verifier-Independent Skill Evolution), a scripts-first approach that uses tool implementations to guide skill revision. It extracts tool capabilities, input requirements, usage conditions, and output formats from source code. Using the task request and execution trace, it compares this information with current workflow instructions to identify missing or conflicting steps. It then recommends specific edits to SKILL.md, linking each change to the relevant implementation and usage conditions. We evaluate VISE as an additional revision stage for four evolution methods on SkillsBench and SkillLearnBench. Compared with the corresponding No-verifier conditions, it improves overall average task success by 9.14-13.35 percentage points. The proportion of tasks solved in all three runs increases by 12.36-18.29 points. A case study shows how revised instructions connect tool outputs to later steps. These results support tool implementations as a practical feedback source for skill self-evolution.

title: The Control-Flow Tax: Specialized Decision Routing for LLM Agent Workflows
abstract: An agent can spend almost as much deciding what to do as doing it. In our documentation workflow, control-flow routing accounts for 42.5% of baseline reference cost on the initial task. Lower token prices alone do not solve this control-flow tax: inexpensive general-purpose routers can trigger additional calls to the expensive generator. We evaluate a heterogeneous architecture in which Jev, a specialized System 1 decision model, controls finite actions while Sol generates documents. Across four software tasks, 480 valid runs comprise 470 completions and ten request-limit endpoints. Jev full routing achieves the lowest mean cost and elapsed time on every task, completing all 40 specialist-controlled runs along the shortest trajectory. On the initial task, mean cost falls by 49.6% (95% paired-bootstrap interval: 42.9% to 56.3%) and elapsed time by 33.2% (19.6% to 46.7%). Across three further tasks, cost reductions are 40.5% to 42.9% and concurrent elapsed-time reductions are 12.9% to 14.4%. Existence-only specialization saves just 1.8% on the initial task. Separately, Sol and Jev each select accepted actions on 100/100 reviewed retail states, with Jev using 97.88% less reference cost and 72.30% less mean request time. The results identify two requirements for efficient agent control: inexpensive decisions and trajectories that preserve those savings.

title: FigmaEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating AI Agents in Professional UI Design
abstract: Recent advances in AI agents have enabled autonomous UI design using professional tools such as Figma, yet evaluating their design capabilities remains challenging due to the open-ended nature of design tasks and the absence of unique ground truths. We introduce FigmaEval, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on professional UI design tasks, comprising 84 tasks and 783 screens derived from real-world Figma design files. FigmaEval adopts a constrained-specification, open-solution paradigm, standardizing task requirements and design resources while allowing agents to independently determine layouts, visual hierarchies, component composition, and visual presentation. To assess design quality beyond reference similarity, we develop 22 expert-grounded evaluation rubrics across six dimensions and introduce a human evaluation arena where professional designers compare agent-generated designs through blinded pairwise judgments. Evaluating eleven models under a unified Figma agent setup, we find substantial agreement between rubric-based assessments and human preferences, alongside distinct differences in design practices and quality--efficiency trade-offs. FigmaEval provides a framework for systematically assessing professional UI design capabilities and understanding the strengths and limitations of current AI agents.

title: SkillCore: Internalizing Generalizable Skills via Scaffolding-Removed Fine-Tuning
abstract: Runtime skills can improve agents' problem-solving capabilities by providing procedural guidance for tasks such as code review and debugging. However, these benefits reach only a minority of users, as most do not proactively invoke skills in practice. We argue that such generalizable procedures should become part of the model's capabilities rather than remain optional external add-ons, making them directly available without explicit skill loading. To this end, we present SkillCore, a data pipeline and supervised fine-tuning recipe for internalizing generalizable skills. We transform real agent trajectories by removing skill-loading scaffolding while preserving the task context and subsequent agent actions, thereby supervising direct execution without external skill content. To preserve access to task-specific skills that provide genuinely external information, we mix these scaffold-removed trajectories with a small proportion of skill-native trajectories that preserve supervision for skill invocation. On a held-out skill-free evaluation, SkillCore improves task completion quality over the base Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-72B models by 54.4% and 24.8%, respectively, while preserving task-specific skill invocation on a separate probe and general coding performance on SWE-bench Verified.

title: From Rule-based to Agentic: LLM Agent based Real-time Control of Urban Drainage Systems for Flooding and Sewer Overflow Mitigation
abstract: Real-time control (RTC) for urban drainage systems (UDS) remains hampered by sparse in-network sensing. While heterogeneous multi-modal meteorological early warnings often contain decision-critical information for UDS RTC, none of the existing approaches can exploit such externally-sourced information within the control workflow. Here we introduce AgenticAI-Control, an agentic artificial intelligence framework able to assimilate multi-source meteorological early warnings in RTC. Two coupled large language model agents are integrated to generate control strategies by retrieving meteorological early-warnings and fusing them with domain engineering expertise. Validated via simulation studies of a combined sewer catchment in eastern China across 10 real-world rainfall events, the AgenticAI-Control achieved 69.1-90.6% reduction in aggregated flood and overflow volumes compared to the rule-based baseline control. Rigorously standardized prompt engineering and modular workflow constraints substantially compress performance disparities among four distinct LLMs. Our work establishes AgenticAI as a viable tool to unify multi-source meteorological monitoring and practitioner domain knowledge, surmounting longstanding monitoring limitations of UDS RTC and delivering cost-efficient, robust intelligent control solutions for sensor-sparse sewer infrastructures.

title: Online Environment Repair for Coding Agents
abstract: Programmatic verifiers provide scalable reward signals for training coding agents with reinforcement learning, yet subtle harness defects and incomplete unit tests allow policies to earn full credit without solving the intended task. Existing training-time defenses intervene either by penalizing suspicious outputs or by filtering flagged tasks and rollouts. However, output penalties leave the underlying verifier exploitable, driving policies to disguise shortcuts under reasoning monitors or zeroing out valid solutions under detector false positives, whereas task and rollout filtering discards or mutes the hardest problems where shortcuts emerge earliest. Pre-training verifier hardening repairs the environment directly, but misses vulnerability classes that surface only as the policy improves during reinforcement learning. In this paper, we propose online environment repair, which leaves triggering rollout rewards unchanged to remove hiding incentives and asynchronously patches exploited environments during training. Candidate repairs triggered by execution invariants or differential fuzzing are deployed only after passing three automated validation gates that block the exploit while preserving valid solutions, canceling detector false positives and enabling structural propagation across repositories without scaffold labels or reference solutions. Across 20 controlled GRPO experiments on heterogeneous software-engineering repositories, online environment repair reduces cumulative reward hacking from 36.9% to 0.06% and improves held-out Pass@8 from 21.7% to 46.7%, consistently outperforming reward-penalty, rollout-filtering, and static-hardening baselines while eliminating zero-shot exploitation on unseen loophole classes.

title: Unifying Partner and Environment Diversity to Improve Human-AI Coordination
abstract: Real-world applications of modern AI systems require generalization to both unseen environments and novel human users. The field of zero-shot coordination (ZSC) has focused primarily on deploying AI to cooperate with novel partners in otherwise familiar environments. Popular population-based methods achieve this by partnering the agent with a diversity of simulated human users during training in a fixed environment, but does not consider the more realistic scenario where both the users and the environment are unseen during training. Recently, training across environments has been explored in training a single self-play agent, which shows better generalization on both novel human users and unseen environments. In this work, we ask whether jointly modeling partner diversity and environment diversity yields stronger coordination with novel partners in novel environments. We introduce Cross Environment Co-Play (CECP), a two-stage framework that first trains a population of self-play agents across a distribution of procedurally generated environments, and then trains a cooperator policy against this partner population. To further couple social and environmental reasoning, we add a next-state prediction module that encourages representations to encode both partner behavior and task structure. We evaluate CECP on both a neuroscience-inspired cooperative foraging task, and the popular ZSC benchmark Overcooked, under held-out partner and held-out environment conditions. CECP achieves the strongest performance among the compared baselines and attains state-of-the-art results under our evaluation protocol for human-AI collaboration. We analyze the model's latent representation encoded by the next-state prediction module, showing it can not only improve the performance of the cooperative AI, but also provide more interpretable latents, demonstrated by the inference of partner skill levels.

title: CAPE: Coordinating Calibration and Search for Tool-Use Policies
abstract: A tool call can fail even when the operation behind it is correct, because the receiving tool parses delimiters, dates or record layouts under a configuration the agent cannot inspect. Compiling a tool-use policy for such a tool requires both calibration, which evaluates candidate calls on candidate configurations, and search over the evaluated calls. The two share one compilation budget: calibrating everything first postpones any improved policy until the end, while re-solving every partially known model delays the next useful query. A call becomes usable as soon as its effects are known on the configurations that reach it. We present CAPE, a training-free compiler built on this observation. It maintains an executable policy at all times, directs calibration to the calls that can improve this policy, and tightens bounds only where doing so ends calibration early. Returned policies preserve every configuration the initial policy completes, and CAPE certifies optimality when its executable and optimistic values meet. On CSV and JSON workflows built from 64 requests, CAPE reaches the independently computed optimum in 502 of 504 compilations while taking 22.0% less compilation time than eager exact search. On larger CSV families it returns policies with higher completion at similar compilation time, and it raises completion by 15.38 to 34.66 percentage points over an LLM that revises its serialization from error feedback.

title: Shuttle: Dependency-Attributed Workflow Evolution for Smart Contract Auditing
abstract: In LLM-based smart contract auditing, detection quality depends on both model capability and workflow design. While coding agents can revise workflows from execution feedback, unconstrained rewrites rarely yield stable gains. Cross-function vulnerabilities require multi-step state tracking and boundary reasoning that coarse pipelines miss. End-to-end outcomes hide which step lost a clue, so direct rewrites regress existing hits or discard valid edits under coarse aggregate scoring. Repeatedly iterating on a small project set also adds case-specific heuristics that bloat prompts and hurt generalization. We present Shuttle, a constrained workflow-evolution system, and LucidScan, the auditing framework it evolves. Shuttle centers on provenance-graph attribution: it expands each run into an instance-level dependency graph, locates the node where a clue was lost via forward search, and traces existing hits backward into a protected set. After evaluating a merged batch, Shuttle drops dragging edits via a node-level provenance ledger, falling back to cache-reusing local re-runs only when early-round edits overlap on the same node. For localized bottlenecks, Shuttle generates edits under task decomposition, progressive refinement, and generality blind review. On 10 training projects, Shuttle evolves LucidScan from $G_0$ (28.7% per-project average C/H/M recall) to $G_8$ (82.1%). On 13 held-out validation projects under the same model, average recall rises from 28.6% ($G_0$) to 70.3% ($G_8$), above Pashov and Codex Security. In an anonymized live public audit contest with 896 researchers (Nov. 2026), the evolved scanner tied for #1 in High-severity recall (6/8, 75.0%), ranked #2 in scored H/M clusters (34/72, 47.2%) with 92.9% validity (78/84), and finished #3 overall.

title: Loupe: Reinforcing Knowledge-Intensive Video Generation Agents
abstract: Knowledge-intensive video generation remains challenging because prompts often omit the facts, appearances, and temporal relationships required for accurate generation. While search-based workflows can retrieve missing evidence, manually designed strategies limit adaptive planning, and conventional training suffers from costly video-level feedback and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment. In this paper, we present Loupe, a video generation agent that retrieves and verifies textual and visual evidence to construct evidence-grounded temporal video prompts with reference images. We further introduce Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which leverages prompt-specific factual, visual, and temporal requirements to evaluate intermediate search and planning decisions before video rendering. Building on RBC, RBC-SFT reweights assistant-token learning by step quality, while RBC-GRPO incorporates step-level credits alongside a final planning reward, without rendering videos during RL. To address the lack of dedicated search-oriented evaluation, we construct Search-VBench, which contains 150 held-out prompts across seven categories. Experiments show that Loupe improves all four evaluation dimensions across three video generators, raising the overall score of MiniMax-H3 from 32.80 to 70.67 and outperforming an untrained search workflow. Ablation experiments show that full RBC training outperforms standard SFT followed by trajectory-level GRPO by 5.27 points. Human evaluations and results on Sci-VBench and KIVI-Bench further demonstrate improved generation quality, scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness. Our project page is available at https://zengkaiya.github.io/Loupe/.

title: Rethinking Video Agents: When and Why Video Harnesses Work
abstract: Video understanding depends not only on how models reason about visual evidence, but also on which evidence they observe. Fixed observation policies determine this evidence in advance; agentic harnesses allow models to seek further observations as their understanding develops. This shift creates an opportunity to realize capabilities that fixed inputs leave untapped, yet the ability to request observations does not ensure their effective use. We investigate when and why video harnesses improve understanding, examining how task demands and models' capacity for interaction jointly shape their benefits. Using Video-Relook as an experimental framework, we let models adapt their temporal and spatial observations from a common default configuration, and analyze performance and interaction trajectories across models and tasks. Adaptive observation yields substantial gains on fine-grained action understanding, with benefits also extending to Video-MME-v2. Even under the same observation interface, gains differ substantially across models; interaction traces reveal corresponding differences in evidence seeking and the reliability of answer revision. The benefits also vary across tasks for the same model, ranging from substantial improvements to limited gains and regressions. Together, these findings support an account in which harness effectiveness depends on the alignment between opportunities for informative observation and the model's ability to turn interaction into reliable revisions. They motivate video harnesses that coordinate perception and reasoning, matching observational autonomy to task demands and model capabilities.

title: Not All Interpretation Methods Are Created Equal: Tiered Evaluation of AI Interpretability
abstract: As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created equal: for interpretability to enhance deployment safety and effectiveness, interpretation methods must be evaluated in a tiered system to differentiate evidence levels of trustworthiness, rather than validated through isolated interpretation instances. Our core vision is that elevating the evaluation of interpretation methods to a core AI assessment metric will drive robust knowledge discovery from data (KDD) and ensure safe, contestable sociotechnical deployments of AI. To this end, we propose TRUST, a tiered evaluation framework that builds upon the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles for Veridical Data Science (VDS) and the Predictive, Descriptive and Relevant (PDR) foundations. To differentiate interpretation methods effectively and systematically, TRUST grades interpretation across five tiers: Task-Aligned PDR Foundations, Rigorous Epistemic Grounding, Unifying Semantic Understanding, Scope Transferability, and Targeted Prospective Validation. We present a start-to-finish case study of the iterative Random Forest (iRF) family under TRUST and contrast it with other LLM interpretation methods that struggle to clear specific tiers. Finally, we conclude with brief initial thoughts on how TRUST principles can extend in autonomous agentic frameworks. Ultimately, the TRUST framework fosters contestability and epistemic grounding as foundational evaluation principles for human-machine workflows and, eventually, autonomous agentic workflows.

title: AGL-SKILL: Coding Harnesses as Agentic Optimizers
abstract: Frontier models are increasingly used through harnesses as agents, with growing autonomy to do useful work. Agent performance can often be enhanced by the use of skills: reusable workflows, code, and prompts that provide task-related information or guide the behaviour of the model. Skills, being textual in nature, present themselves as another editable surface to be optimized; current methods have improved on handcrafting and one-shot generation by treating skill development as an iterative process, using score-driven search to tweak and improve performance. In this paper, we demonstrate the efficacy of the agents themselves as optimizers: across five benchmarks, a coding agent without guidance substantially improves every target and outperforms published skill-optimization methods. More broadly, this shows the capability of agents to do such work and to refine their own behaviour to provide task-specific context, as long as they are given a metric to measure against.

title: TACT-Bench: Testing Adaptive Conversational Threats against Tool-Use Agents
abstract: The growing autonomy of AI agents in using external tools and making decisions has created an urgent need for comprehensive safety benchmarks. Existing benchmarks test compromised tool channels or adaptive multi-turn attacks, though they may not capture the unique capabilities of policy-governed tool-use agents, which must resist unauthorized requests without abandoning the legitimate work embedded in the same interaction. To fill this gap, we introduce TACT-Bench, a stateful benchmark built around scenario-specific stories, personas, manipulation tactics, and response-adaptive escalation. Each adversarial task targets an action explicitly prohibited by the policy provided to the assistant, while the policy remains hidden from the attacking user. TACT pairs each adversarial task with at least one benign counterpart, and its adversarial tasks retain authorized ground-truth actions when a compliant resolution remains available. We define these base tasks as TACT-Base. We additionally introduce TACT-TrustPrime, which places an independent benign task before an unrelated attack in the same conversation. We also propose Paired Selective Trustworthiness (PST), which combines explicit safe refusal with demonstrated capability on matched benign tasks, to analyze an agent's overcautiousness and practicality. Averaged across 6 different models as assistants, TACT-Base raises Attack-Induced Failure Rate (AFR) by 17.53% over four compatible attack baselines, and TACT-TrustPrime raises it by a further 17.01%. The two evaluated defense methods reduce AFR by only 8.35%--9.41% on average and do not consistently improve PST, underscoring the need for stronger policy-enforcement methods.

title: Where is the Interface for the AI Harness?
abstract: Norman's gulfs of execution and evaluation have guided interaction design for forty years, but both assume a user who is present in the loop. Agentic delegation breaks that assumption: users describe an outcome and leave, while the agent takes hundreds of unseen actions. Starting from a 2026 incident in which a research agent circumvented an access refusal on an Australian government portal and went unnoticed for two months, we argue that delegation opens two new gulfs. The gulf of specification is the gap between what a user wants and their ability to express it, including how the agent should behave in situations nobody foresaw. The gulf of oversight is the gap between what an agent is doing and the user's ability to know, assess, and control it. We argue that both gulfs meet in the harness, the tools, permissions, checks, and loop that surround the model. Harnesses are currently written by developers and hidden from users. We call on HCI to decide which parts of the harness belong to the end-user, which should be visible and adjustable defaults, and which should be built in by design, and to create the interfaces that let ordinary people author and read them.

title: Reproducing History Is Not Enough: Intervention-Level Assurance for LLM-Generated Simulators
abstract: Large language models can now write simulation programs of operational processes and workflows. These programs can be reused to answer what-if questions on new records and policies. However, a program that reproduces recorded history can still give wrong answers to what-if questions; requested changes may be applied wrongly, or they may be applied to records other than the ones the question is about, or the program may stop being valid once its policy is revised. Current checks return a pass-or-fail verdict for the whole program, which says little about whether any single answer can be trusted. We propose Vouch, a library that judges whether an answer from a generated simulator can be trusted for the change being asked about. Each what-if question is turned into a structured change, which is checked against the program and the current records. The library also keeps a record of the kinds of change each program has passed or failed, and repeats the relevant tests whenever the program is reused. We apply it to three program-generation platforms, with programs built by five language models, across four domains: manufacturing, IT operations, and pharmacy and loan-application workflows, using independently checked reference answers. Our baselines are the platforms' own checks where such checks exist, an LLM-as-a-judge, and a ReAct agent that can run the program. We measure how many correct answers are trusted, how many are wrongly rejected, how many wrong answers are accepted, and what the checking costs.   On programs written by Haiku and Sonnet in one platform, Vouch removes 97.6% of the wrong answers, while still trusting 80.1% of all answers. At equal coverage, it accepts fewer wrong answers than LLM judges built on Claude Haiku. We disclose code and results for reproducibility.

title: SecondChance: Benchmarking Reliable Error Recovery in AI Agents
abstract: AI agents make errors while they act, and their reliability depends on what they do afterwards. Existing recovery benchmarks mostly inject faults, involve no user and score whether the task is eventually completed, so they cannot show whether an agent undid its own silent error, told the user, or faced an error that could not be fixed. We introduce SecondChance, an error checkpoint dataset and evaluation harness that profiles and measures error-recovery behaviour of AI agents. The errors are natural: they come from agents' own task attempts in $τ^2$-bench, BFCL and AppWorld. Different agents then resume from the same checkpoints under one of four conditions: no assistance, an error notice, the error location, or repair guidance. We measure error correction, task success, policy compliance, preservation of environment state, repair durability and cost. We evaluate 12 models under all four conditions in 5,760 continuations. Recovery is rare: across its environments, the best model completes only 16% of recoveries unaided and 27% with repair guidance. Correcting is not recovering: with repair guidance, Llama-3.3-70B corrects 26% of $τ^2$ errors but completes none, and 40 of 84 successful AppWorld continuations leave the error in place. SecondChance exposes these differences that task success alone cannot capture.

title: LatentLens: Rethinking Latent Interface in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Latent interfaces let agents in a multi-agent system communicate through continuous representations rather than decoded text. Prior work reports performance and efficiency gains, but neither separates latent communication from the agent harness nor examines its internal components, leaving its actual contribution unclear. We propose LatentLens, a framework that decouples the latent interface at two levels: externally from the agent harness, to measure its contribution to overall performance (RQ1), and internally into realignment compatibility, information accessibility, and propagation dynamics, to identify the benefits and limitations of each (RQ2). Across seven benchmarks with Qwen3 models, adding the latent interface to the same harness does not improve and can even substantially degrade accuracy. Internally, latent representations retain some domain information, but incompatible realignment can substantially degrade performance, and repeated latent steps can amplify representation-level failures. Thus, while latent representations may preserve information, they do not necessarily ensure effective communication, which also requires compatible realignment, information accessibility, and stable propagation.

title: Off-the-Shelf Autonomous Agents for Game Playtesting
abstract: In playtesting games, a human operator is typically required to test most gameplay elements. In this work we present Buddy, an autonomous game solving agent which can solve long time horizon objectives in an unseen 3D role-playing game using off-the-shelf language model systems. Buddy will take actions, receive feedback on those actions, and pursue a goal across many turns. No written walkthrough or model training of any kind is required, and we show that this paradigm holds in a novel environment where the agent must discover solutions via exploration rather than recalling them from pretraining. We demonstrate three downstream capabilities: game solving with no provided walkthrough, logging bug tickets for encountered difficulties, and conversion of successful agent traces into scripted hierarchical task networks for regression testing. Unlike existing playtesting solutions, our framework is fully modular: language models and harnesses can be easily swapped out as capabilities improve over time.

title: PatientFlowSynth: Evaluating FHIR Agents with Matched Patient Charts
abstract: Agents that search patient charts must classify claims from retrieved records, including cases with missing or conflicting evidence. In Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR), status fields can change how those records should be interpreted. PatientFlowSynth provides 18,000 tasks from 225 synthetic patients and 18 templates that hold the patient, question, and retrieval program fixed across chart variants representing four evidence states. Re-executing the program verifies each variant's reference answer, evidence sets, and search requirements. Strict success requires a completed response with correct labels and citations exactly matching an accepted evidence set retrieved during the episode. Where required, a tool response must also show a complete search at the specified scope. In a study using GPT-5.6 Luna and 225 synthetic patients (3,600 matched pairs), explicit Encounter-status guidance increased strict success from 40.7% to 51.3% (+10.6 percentage points; 95% patient-bootstrap confidence interval, 8.4 to 12.8). Among cases whose primary reference label was insufficient evidence, label agreement fell from 49.2% to 29.3%. A prespecified two-model replication reproduced both changes. Failed retrieval can mask interpretation errors by producing a correct insufficient-evidence label without examining the relevant records. Additional model comparisons showed that the benefit of guidance was model-dependent. Retrieval, citation, and classification should be evaluated separately.

title: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop
abstract: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: https://ghadinehme.com/robobuilder.github.io/

title: Can Language Models Build Molecules in Three Dimensions?
abstract: Chemical drawings convey which atoms are bonded and how stereocentres are configured, but not molecular shape. Every simulation starts from three-dimensional coordinates, and building them from a drawing remains a manual step. We introduce MolDraft, a curated benchmark of 300 drawing-structure pairs spanning natural products, hypervalent compounds, and coordination complexes. Given an image and a short instruction, an AI system must generate a complete set of atomic coordinates, which are checked for molecular identity, stereochemical configuration, and coarse ligand geometry. We evaluate nine multimodal language models using the same agent setup. The share of molecules built correctly, the resolve rate, ranges from 25.0% to 76.0% and falls as molecules grow, most sharply above about 80 atoms. Only 29 of the 300 molecules are resolved by all nine models, and literature structures, mostly metal complexes, are the hardest source for every model. Language models can thus build many molecules in three dimensions, but not yet reliably reproduce the coordination chemistry of the research literature.
